claim: The Arabidopsis genome encodes two groups of 14-3-3s, one of which – epsilon – is thought to fulfill conserved cellular functions.
source: The Arabidopsis genome encodes two groups of 14-3-3s, one of which – epsilon – is thought to fulfill conserved cellular functions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge about 14-3-3 protein classification and evolutionary conservation.

claim: Simultaneous and conditional repression of 14-3-3 epsilon group members by RNA interference and artificial microRNA in seedlings led to altered distribution patterns of the phytohormone auxin.
source: Their simultaneous and conditional repression by RNA interference and artificial microRNA in seedlings led to altered distribution patterns of the phytohormone auxin and associated auxin transport-related phenotypes, such as agravitropic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the RNAi and amiRNA experiments described in the manuscript, including DR5 reporter analysis.

claim: Simultaneous and conditional repression of 14-3-3 epsilon group members led to auxin transport-related phenotypes, such as agravitropic growth.
source: Their simultaneous and conditional repression by RNA interference and artificial microRNA in seedlings led to altered distribution patterns of the phytohormone auxin and associated auxin transport-related phenotypes, such as agravitropic growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of seedling growth patterns shown in figures.

claim: 14-3-3 epsilon members were required for pronounced polar distribution of PIN-FORMED auxin efflux carriers within the plasma membrane.
source: Moreover, 14-3-3 epsilon members were required for pronounced polar distribution of PIN-FORMED auxin efflux carriers within the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing PIN protein localization in wild-type versus mutant backgrounds.

claim: Defects in defined post-Golgi trafficking processes proved causal for the PIN polarity phenotype.
source: Defects in defined post-Golgi trafficking processes proved causal for this phenotype and might be due to lack of direct 14-3-3 interactions with factors crucial for membrane trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using trafficking inhibitors and FM4-64 dye experiments.

claim: The defects in post-Golgi trafficking might be due to lack of direct 14-3-3 interactions with factors crucial for membrane trafficking.
source: Defects in defined post-Golgi trafficking processes proved causal for this phenotype and might be due to lack of direct 14-3-3 interactions with factors crucial for membrane trafficking.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on co-immunoprecipitation data identifying trafficking-related proteins.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana expresses thirteen 14-3-3 isoforms which can be divided into two major phylogenetic groups, the non-epsilon group (eight members) and the ancestral epsilon group (five members).
source: Arabidopsis thaliana expresses thirteen 14-3-3 isoforms which can be divided into two major phylogenetic groups, the non-epsilon group (eight members) and the ancestral epsilon group (five members) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A and established knowledge from literature.

claim: Members of both epsilon and non-epsilon groups are present in all plant genomes sequenced so far.
source: Members of both groups are present in all plant genomes sequenced so far.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis across multiple plant species shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Except for the moss P. patens, the total transcript level of all non-epsilon members in a given plant species is generally higher than that of the epsilon group isoforms.
source: Except for the moss, P. patens, the total transcript level of all non-epsilon members in a given plant species is generally higher than that of the epsilon group isoforms.
evidence: This is based on publicly accessible RNA-seq or microarray data as stated in the text.

claim: The ancestral epsilon group may mediate fundamental cellular features while non-epsilon members may perform organism-specific functions.
source: The ancestral epsilon group may mediate fundamental cellular features while non-epsilon members may perform organism-specific functions (Ferl et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Ferl et al., 2002.

claim: The Arabidopsis 14-3-3 isoform kappa (non-epsilon) is required for PHOTOTROPIN2-mediated blue-light-induced stomatal opening.
source: In this regard, it has recently been shown that the Arabidopsis 14-3-3 isoform kappa (non-epsilon) is required for PHOTOTROPIN2-mediated blue-light-induced stomatal opening (Tseng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tseng et al., 2012.

claim: The knockout mutant of upsilon flowers late under long day conditions.
source: However, with the exception of upsilon, the knockout mutant of which flowers late under long day conditions (Mayfield et al., 2012), several single and double T-DNA-induced loss-of-function alleles of non-epsilon isoforms are indistinguishable from wild type under normal growth conditions and even quadruple mutants showed only a mild reduction of primary root length (van Kleeff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mayfield et al., 2012.

claim: Several single and double T-DNA-induced loss-of-function alleles of non-epsilon isoforms are indistinguishable from wild type under normal growth conditions.
source: However, with the exception of upsilon, the knockout mutant of which flowers late under long day conditions (Mayfield et al., 2012), several single and double T-DNA-induced loss-of-function alleles of non-epsilon isoforms are indistinguishable from wild type under normal growth conditions and even quadruple mutants showed only a mild reduction of primary root length (van Kleeff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Kleeff et al., 2014.

claim: Quadruple mutants of non-epsilon isoforms showed only a mild reduction of primary root length.
source: However, with the exception of upsilon, the knockout mutant of which flowers late under long day conditions (Mayfield et al., 2012), several single and double T-DNA-induced loss-of-function alleles of non-epsilon isoforms are indistinguishable from wild type under normal growth conditions and even quadruple mutants showed only a mild reduction of primary root length (van Kleeff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Kleeff et al., 2014.

claim: Under given abiotic stress conditions, a certain specificity of defined double mutants was uncovered.
source: Nevertheless, under given abiotic stress conditions, a certain specificity of defined double mutants was uncovered (van Kleeff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Kleeff et al., 2014.

claim: Functional overlap seems to be a predominant issue among non-epsilon 14-3-3 members.
source: Taken together, functional overlap seems to be a predominant issue among non-epsilon 14-3-3 members.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing mild phenotypes in multiple mutants.

claim: Expression of iota (AT1G26480) is restricted to pollen.
source: Expression of iota (AT1G26480) is restricted to pollen, while pi (AT1G78220) is exclusively expressed in anthers and the chalazal cyst of the seed (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Pi (AT1G78220) is exclusively expressed in anthers and the chalazal cyst of the seed.
source: Expression of iota (AT1G26480) is restricted to pollen, while pi (AT1G78220) is exclusively expressed in anthers and the chalazal cyst of the seed (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: Omicron (AT1G34760) is expressed in anthers, roots and cotyledons.
source: Yet another epsilon group member, omicron (AT1G34760), is expressed in anthers too, but also moderately in roots and cotyledons.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis of transgenic reporter lines.

claim: The expression of the remaining 10 non-epsilon and epsilon isoforms occurs in neither a tissue-specific nor a developmentally regulated manner.
source: Overall, however, the expression of the remaining 10 non-epsilon and epsilon isoforms occurs in neither a tissue-specific nor a developmentally regulated manner (isoform nu shown in Figure 1H–O).
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 1H-O for nu as an example.

claim: In Arabidopsis, differences in the expression patterns of 14-3-3 isoforms are not assumed to contribute to possible isoform specificity.
source: Thus, in Arabidopsis, differences in the expression patterns of 14-3-3 isoforms are not assumed to contribute to possible isoform specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most isoforms are ubiquitously expressed.

claim: The same applies to the majority of isoforms expressed in S. lycopersicum, M. truncatula, P. trichocarpa, O. sativa and P. patens.
source: The same applies to the majority of isoforms expressed in S. lycopersicum, M. truncatula, P. trichocarpa, O. sativa and P. patens (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on publicly accessible expression data analyzed and presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: A knockdown of the 14-3-3 isoform mu (SALK_004455) caused significantly shorter roots in constant light.
source: It has previously been reported that a knockdown of the 14-3-3 isoform mu (SALK_004455) caused significantly shorter roots in constant light (Mayfield et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mayfield et al., 2012.

claim: The homozygous SALK line (SALK_004455) did not show a striking phenotype under the authors' growth conditions.
source: The homozygous SALK line, however, did not show a striking phenotype in our hands (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; see also: [Cao et al., 2007; He et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Semiquantitative RT-PCR confirmed that the expression of the targeted 14-3-3 isoforms was efficiently reduced upon ethanol treatment.
source: Semiquantitative RT-PCR confirmed that the expression of the targeted 14-3-3 isoforms was efficiently reduced upon ethanol treatment (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Transcript levels of all non-epsilon isoforms were unaffected in emo-RNAi lines.
source: Notably, transcript levels of all non-epsilon isoforms were unaffected (kappa, chi, upsilon shown in Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Under inductive conditions (0.1%(v/v) ethanol), emo-RNAi and amiRNA-(em)o seedlings were strongly defective in growth, with highly impaired root elongation and nonexpanded, epinastic cotyledons.
source: Under inductive conditions (0.1%(v/v) ethanol), emo-RNAi (Figure 2B) and amiRNA-(em)o (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) seedlings were strongly defective in growth, with highly impaired root elongation and nonexpanded, epinastic cotyledons.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Etiolated emo-RNAi seedlings germinated on inductive medium showed a severe defect in elongation of both roots and hypocotyls.
source: Etiolated emo-RNAi seedlings germinated on inductive medium showed a severe defect in elongation of both roots and hypocotyls (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ethylene overproduction is not the underlying cause of the emo-RNAi phenotype since the biosynthesis inhibitor aminovinylglycine (AVG) does not rescue the phenotype.
source: Ethylene overproduction is not the underlying cause since the biosynthesis inhibitor aminovinylglycine (AVG) does not rescue the phenotype (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The hypocotyls of emo-RNAi are hookless even in the presence of the ethylene biosynthesis precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC).
source: In addition, the hypocotyls are hookless even in the presence of the ethylene biosynthesis precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both apical hook development and ethylene-induced hook exaggeration have been most extensively connected with auxin.
source: Both apical hook development and ethylene-induced hook exaggeration have been most extensively connected with auxin (Stepanova et al., 2008; Vandenbussche et al., 2010; Zádníková et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stepanova et al., 2008; Vandenbussche et al., 2010; Zádníková et al., 2010.

claim: Light grown emo-RNAi/amiRNA(em)o seedlings exhibit a wavy root phenotype and do not form lateral roots.
source: Taking into account that light grown emo-RNAi/amiRNA(em)o seedlings exhibit a wavy root phenotype and do not form lateral roots, the phenotypic features might be related to alterations in auxin-mediated processes.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations of the mutant seedlings.

claim: Auxin-induced gene expression was not severely affected in roots of the mutant following ethanol treatment.
source: Auxin-induced gene expression was not severely affected in roots of the mutant following ethanol treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that auxin perception and the subsequent degradation of Aux/IAA repressors were not compromised.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Auxin perception and the subsequent degradation of Aux/IAA repressors were not compromised in emo-RNAi.
source: Auxin-induced gene expression was not severely affected in roots of the mutant following ethanol treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that auxin perception and the subsequent degradation of Aux/IAA repressors were not compromised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that auxin-induced gene expression was not severely affected.

claim: Upon ethanol treatment (3 days) in the presence of NAA (48 hr), discrete lateral root primordia formed along the main root of control seedlings.
source: Upon ethanol treatment (3 days) in the presence of the transportable synthetic auxin naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) (48 hr), discrete lateral root primordia formed along the main root of control seedlings (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: emo1-RNAi seedlings displayed highly disorganized proliferation of pericycle cells in response to NAA treatment.
source: By contrast, emo1-RNAi seedlings displayed highly disorganized proliferation of pericycle cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The disorganized proliferation of pericycle cells in emo1-RNAi resembles wild-type roots treated with the non-transportable auxin analogue 2,4-dichlorphenoxyacetic acid (2,4D).
source: This resembles wild-type roots treated with the non-transportable auxin analogue 2,4-dichlorphenoxyacetic acid (2,4D) (Figure 3C) (Geldner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data shown in Figure 3C and citation to Geldner et al., 2004.

claim: emo1-RNAi roots failed to orient their growth with respect to the gravity vector.
source: In addition, emo1-RNAi roots failed to orient their growth with respect to the gravity vector (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D) and moreover, etiolated seedlings had agravitropic hypocotyls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropism assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: Etiolated emo1-RNAi seedlings had agravitropic hypocotyls.
source: In addition, emo1-RNAi roots failed to orient their growth with respect to the gravity vector (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D) and moreover, etiolated seedlings had agravitropic hypocotyls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G.

claim: Wildtype seedlings spontaneously regenerated a root from the hypocotyl stump after surgical removal of the primary root, while emo1-RNAi seedlings were unable to form adventitious roots.
source: As expected, wildtype seedlings spontaneously regenerated a root from the hypocotyl stump, while emo1-RNAi seedlings were unable to form adventitious roots (Figure 2—figure supplement 3M–P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3M–P.

claim: The function of 14-3-3 epsilon group members is required for auxin-transport-dependent development in both roots and shoots.
source: Together, these data show that the function of 14-3-3 epsilon group members is required for auxin-transport-dependent development in both roots and shoots.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations including gravitropism, lateral root formation, and adventitious root formation.

claim: In wild-type root meristems, DR5 was highly active in the columella and in stele tissues.
source: In wild-type root meristems, DR5 was highly active in the columella and in stele tissues (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by DR5::GUS reporter data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Induction of emo1-RNAi caused an ectopic accumulation of GUS activity in the entire lateral root cap.
source: By contrast, induction of emo1-RNAi caused an ectopic accumulation of GUS activity (Figure 3J) / expression of GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) in the entire lateral root cap.
evidence: This is supported by DR5 reporter data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Roots have homeostatic mechanisms that maintain the endogenous auxin gradients in the presence of exogenously applied auxin.
source: As reported previously, roots have homeostatic mechanisms that maintain the endogenous auxin gradients in the presence of exogenously applied auxin (Geldner et al., 2004; Friml et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geldner et al., 2004 and Friml et al., 2002.

claim: Exposure to low concentrations of the transportable auxin NAA did not lead to strong alterations in DR5::GUS staining in control roots.
source: Exposure to low concentrations of the transportable auxin NAA did hence not lead to strong alterations in DR5::GUS staining in control roots (Figure 3H,I), whereas GUS activity expanded across the entire root of emo1-RNAi seedlings (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is supported by DR5::GUS reporter data shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: GUS activity expanded across the entire root of emo1-RNAi seedlings upon NAA treatment.
source: Exposure to low concentrations of the transportable auxin NAA did hence not lead to strong alterations in DR5::GUS staining in control roots (Figure 3H,I), whereas GUS activity expanded across the entire root of emo1-RNAi seedlings (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is supported by DR5::GUS reporter data shown in Figure 3K,L.

claim: emo roots have a reduced capacity to maintain auxin gradients in the presence of exogenous auxin.
source: Apparently, emo roots have a reduced capacity to maintain auxin gradients in the presence of exogenous auxin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that GUS activity expanded across the entire root upon NAA treatment.

claim: After gravistimulation of the wild type, the DR5rev::GFP signal relocated asymmetrically to the gravistimulated side.
source: After gravistimulation of the wild type, the DR5rev::GFP signal relocated asymmetrically to the gravistimulated side (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,G), indicating a shift in auxin distribution which is essential for the differential growth response (Ottenschläger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by DR5rev::GFP reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,G.

claim: The shift in auxin distribution after gravistimulation is essential for the differential growth response.
source: After gravistimulation of the wild type, the DR5rev::GFP signal relocated asymmetrically to the gravistimulated side (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,G), indicating a shift in auxin distribution which is essential for the differential growth response (Ottenschläger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ottenschläger et al., 2003.

claim: The ectopic lateral expression pattern of DR5rev::GFP in the root meristem of emo1-RNAi persisted, independent of gravistimulation.
source: By contrast, the ectopic lateral expression pattern of DR5rev::GFP in the root meristem of emo1-RNAi persisted, independent of gravistimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by DR5rev::GFP reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Interference with 14-3-3 epsilon group members affects auxin distribution.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that interference with 14-3-3 epsilon group members affects auxin distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple DR5 reporter experiments.

claim: Auxin transport to the root tip decreased upon ethanol induction in emo1-RNAi (24 hr: 22%, 48 hr: 42%).
source: As compared with the non-induced emo1-RNAi control, auxin transport to the root tip decreased upon ethanol induction (Figure 2—figure supplements 3E, 24 hr: 22%, 48 hr: 42%, n = 10) and, furthermore, the gradual decrease in auxin response gradients within the root tip could be visualized by using the DR5rev::GFP reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by radioactive auxin transport assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The gradual decrease in auxin response gradients within the root tip could be visualized by using the DR5rev::GFP reporter.
source: As compared with the non-induced emo1-RNAi control, auxin transport to the root tip decreased upon ethanol induction (Figure 2—figure supplements 3E, 24 hr: 22%, 48 hr: 42%, n = 10) and, furthermore, the gradual decrease in auxin response gradients within the root tip could be visualized by using the DR5rev::GFP reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by DR5rev::GFP reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: An epinasty cotyledon phenotype is characteristic of auxin overproducers.
source: However, another striking aspect of the RNAi-mutant upon transfer to ethanol-containing medium is an epinasty cotyledon phenotype (Figure 2B), characteristic of auxin overproducers (Zhao et al., 2001; Boerjan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2001 and Boerjan et al., 1995.

claim: The auxin level might be elevated in emo hypocotyls and cotyledons.
source: Consequently, in contrast to the situation in roots, the auxin level might be elevated in emo hypocotyls and cotyledons.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the epinasty phenotype and DR5 reporter activity.

claim: The mutant showed a severe increase in DR5::GUS reporter activity in the cotyledons upon induction.
source: Accordingly, the mutant showed a severe increase in DR5::GUS reporter activity in the cotyledons upon induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3L).
evidence: This is supported by DR5::GUS reporter data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3L.

claim: Treatment of the wild type with the auxin transport inhibitor NPA resulted in agravitropic hypocotyls.
source: Intriguingly, treatment of the wild type with the auxin transport inhibitor NPA resulted in agravitropic hypocotyls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H), an increase in GUS activity in cotyledons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J) and the formation of epinastic leaves (Geldner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3H.

claim: Treatment of the wild type with NPA resulted in an increase in GUS activity in cotyledons.
source: Intriguingly, treatment of the wild type with the auxin transport inhibitor NPA resulted in agravitropic hypocotyls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H), an increase in GUS activity in cotyledons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J) and the formation of epinastic leaves (Geldner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by DR5::GUS reporter data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3J.

claim: Treatment of the wild type with NPA resulted in the formation of epinastic leaves.
source: Intriguingly, treatment of the wild type with the auxin transport inhibitor NPA resulted in agravitropic hypocotyls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H), an increase in GUS activity in cotyledons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J) and the formation of epinastic leaves (Geldner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geldner et al., 2004.

claim: Suppression of 14-3-3 expression impairs auxin transport in both roots and aerial tissues, resulting in depletion of auxin in the root tip and an elevated auxin level in the apical part.
source: Taken together, this strongly suggests that suppression of 14-3-3 expression impairs auxin transport in both roots and aerial tissues, resulting in depletion of auxin in the root tip and an elevated auxin level in the apical part.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations including DR5 reporter activity and auxin transport assays.

claim: According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis for polar auxin transport, the activity of the PM localized H+-ATPase is crucial for auxin uptake into the cell and, consequently, directed cellular export mediated by auxin efflux facilitators.
source: According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis for polar auxin transport, the activity of the PM localized H+-ATPase is crucial for auxin uptake into the cell and, consequently, directed cellular export mediated by auxin efflux facilitators.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemiosmotic hypothesis.

claim: Regulation of the H+-ATPase is one of the most highly explored functions of plant 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Regulation of this P-type proton pump is one of the most highly explored functions of plant 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature on plant 14-3-3 proteins.

claim: Phosphorylation-dependent association of 14-3-3 with the penultimate residue of the H+-ATPase results in a displacement of the C-terminal autoinhibitor and hence activation of the pump.
source: In brief, phosphorylation-dependent association of 14-3-3 with the penultimate residue results in a displacement of the C-terminal autoinhibitor and hence activation of the pump (Speth et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Speth et al., 2010.

claim: Dexamethasone (Dex)-dependent expression of AHA2Δ94 did not rescue the emo1-RNAi phenotype.
source: Dexamethasone (Dex)-dependent expression of one of the major H+-ATPase isoforms, AHA2, deleted of its C-terminal autoinhibitor (94 amino acids, 1-887, AHA2Δ94) (Pacheco-Villalobos et al., 2016) and thus representing a constitutively active version of the H+-pump uncoupled from regulatory inputs, did not rescue the emo1-RNAi phenotype (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: The effects observed in wild type upon Dex treatment (shorter hypocotyls, absence of an apical hook and open cotyledons) are the consequence of an activation of the H+-ATPase.
source: Notably, the effects observed in wild type upon Dex treatment (shorter hypocotyls, absence of an apical hook and open cotyledons) are indeed the consequence of an activation of the H+-ATPase since they can be mimicked by a specific activator of the H+-pump, fusicoccin (Würtele et al., 2003) (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G and citation to Würtele et al., 2003.

claim: Inhibition of the H+-ATPase is not the underlying cause of the emo1-RNAi phenotype.
source: Therefore, inhibition of the H+-ATPase is not the underlying cause of the emo1-RNAi phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiment with constitutively active AHA2.

claim: Interaction of 14-3-3 epsilon and the PIN2 hydrophilic loop (amino acids 187-477) was not detectable by yeast two-hybrid assay and ratiometric bimolecular fluorescence complementation in planta.
source: Interaction of 14-3-3 epsilon and the PIN2 hydrophilic loop (amino acids 187-477) was not detectable by yeast two-hybrid assay and ratiometric bimolecular fluorescence complementation in planta (Grefen and Blatt, 2012) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, PIN1-GFP was detected predominantly at the basal side of stele and endodermis cells of the wild type with occasional weak expression in cortex cells.
source: Under our experimental conditions, PIN1-GFP (pPIN1:PIN1-GFP, [Benková et al., 2003]) was detected predominantly at the basal side of stele and endodermis cells of the wild type with occasional weak expression in cortex cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: PIN2-GFP is expressed in older epidermis and cortex cells exhibiting apical and basal polarity, respectively.
source: PIN2-GFP (pPIN2:PIN2-GFP; [Xu and Scheres, 2005]) is expressed in older epidermis and cortex cells exhibiting apical and basal polarity, respectively (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Interference with 14-3-3 function resulted in misexpression of PIN1-GFP and PIN2-GFP.
source: Interference with 14-3-3 function resulted in misexpression of the two auxin efflux carriers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on microscopy observations of PIN-GFP expression patterns.

claim: PIN1-GFP fluorescence was observed in cortex cells with an intensity comparable to that in endodermis cells and also moderately in the epidermis in emo1-RNAi.
source: PIN1-GFP fluorescence was observed in cortex cells with an intensity comparable to that in endodermis cells and also moderately in the epidermis (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: PIN2-GFP showed misexpression in the younger epidermis and cortex daughter cells and in the entire lateral root cap in emo1-RNAi.
source: PIN2-GFP showed misexpression in the younger epidermis and cortex daughter cells and in the entire lateral root cap as well (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Crossregulation of PIN gene expression has been described in pin mutants or plants with inhibited auxin transport.
source: Crossregulation of PIN gene expression has been described in pin mutants or plants with inhibited auxin transport (Vieten et al., 2005) and thus, the defects observed in emo1-RNAi roots are probably the consequence of the interference with auxin homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vieten et al., 2005.

claim: The defects in PIN expression observed in emo1-RNAi roots are probably the consequence of the interference with auxin homeostasis.
source: Crossregulation of PIN gene expression has been described in pin mutants or plants with inhibited auxin transport (Vieten et al., 2005) and thus, the defects observed in emo1-RNAi roots are probably the consequence of the interference with auxin homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known crossregulation of PIN genes.

claim: The subcellular polar localization of PIN-GFP proteins was reduced as a consequence of RNAi induction.
source: Notably, the subcellular polar localization of PIN-GFP proteins was reduced as a consequence of RNAi induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on microscopy observations of PIN-GFP localization.

claim: In emo1-RNAi, the PIN1-GFP signal was not restricted to the basal side of those cells showing misexpression.
source: In emo1-RNAi, the PIN1-GFP signal was not restricted to the basal side of those cells showing misexpression.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations.

claim: PIN1-GFP was additionally detectable in the outer lateral PM-side of endodermal cells and did not show pronounced polarity in cortex cells in emo1-RNAi.
source: In fact, PIN1-GFP was additionally detectable in the outer lateral PM-side of endodermal cells and did not show pronounced polarity in cortex cells (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: By contrast with the wild type, PIN2-GFP fluorescence is frequently visible in the inner lateral PM-side of cortex cells upon interference with 14-3-3 function.
source: Moreover, by contrast with the wild type, PIN2-GFP fluorescence is frequently visible in the inner lateral PM-side of cortex cells upon interference with 14-3-3 function (Figure 5F,H).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5F,H.

claim: PIN proteins continuously cycle between endosomes and the PM via vesicle trafficking allowing for the establishment and rapid alteration of polarity.
source: PIN proteins continuously cycle between endosomes and the PM via vesicle trafficking allowing for the establishment and rapid alteration of polarity (Geldner et al., 2004; Dhonukshe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geldner et al., 2004 and Dhonukshe et al., 2007.

claim: PIN proteins are sorted to the lytic vacuole via late endosomes (LE)/multivesicular bodies (MVB), resulting in protein degradation and modulation of auxin fluxes.
source: Furthermore, PIN proteins are sorted to the lytic vacuole via late endosomes (LE)/multivesicular bodies (MVB), resulting in protein degradation and modulation of auxin fluxes (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008.

claim: Brefeldin A (BFA) causes PIN accumulation in intracellular, so-called BFA compartments encompassing aggregation of early endosomes (EE)/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and recycling endosomes that get surrounded by MVBs and the golgi apparatus.
source: Accordingly, treatment with vesicle trafficking inhibitors affects PIN trafficking/localization: Brefeldin A (BFA) causes PIN accumulation in intracellular, so-called BFA compartments encompassing aggregation of early endosomes (EE)/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and recycling endosomes that get surrounded by MVBs and the golgi apparatus (Robinson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robinson et al., 2008.

claim: The BFA-induced PIN2-GFP accumulation was more pronounced in ethanol-treated root epidermis cells of emo1-RNAi as compared to the wild type.
source: We noticed that the BFA-induced PIN2-GFP accumulation was more pronounced in ethanol-treated root epidermis cells of emo1-RNAi as compared to the wild type (Figure 6A–F,K), irrespective of the presence of the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) (Figure 6G,I).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A–F,K.

claim: A comparable scenario of enhanced BFA-induced PIN accumulation has been described for ric1-1 and bex5-1 mutants, which are affected in endocytosis and PIN recycling to the plasma membrane, respectively.
source: A comparable scenario has been described for ric1-1 (Chen et al., 2012) and bex5-1 (Feraru et al., 2012) mutants, which are affected in endocytosis and PIN recycling to the plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012 and Feraru et al., 2012.

claim: Endocytosis does not seem to be significantly altered in emo1-RNAi as evidenced by short-term uptake of the endocytic tracer FM4-64.
source: Endocytosis, however, does not seem to be significantly altered in emo1-RNAi as evidenced by short-term uptake of the endocytic tracer FM4-64 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 uptake data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,D.

claim: The mutant displayed BFA hypersensitivity even when treated with 10 μM BFA.
source: Strikingly, the mutant displayed BFA hypersensitivity even when treated with 10 μM BFA (Figure 6L), a concentration which preferentially inhibits recycling and minimizes the interference with vacuolar trafficking (Robert et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: 10 μM BFA preferentially inhibits recycling and minimizes the interference with vacuolar trafficking.
source: Strikingly, the mutant displayed BFA hypersensitivity even when treated with 10 μM BFA (Figure 6L), a concentration which preferentially inhibits recycling and minimizes the interference with vacuolar trafficking (Robert et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robert et al., 2010 and Chen et al., 2012.

claim: Exocytosis might be affected in emo1-RNAi.
source: This suggests that exocytosis might be affected in emo1-RNAi.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on BFA hypersensitivity at low concentrations.

claim: The PIN2-containing BFA compartments efficiently disappeared in wild-type root epidermal cells after BFA washout (washout efficiency: 66%).
source: While the PIN2-containing BFA compartments efficiently disappeared in wild-type root epidermal cells (washout efficiency: 66%, n ≥ 100 cells, 20 roots), BFA-induced PIN2-GFP agglomerations persisted in emo1-RNAi (washout efficiency: 39%, n ≥ 100 cells, 20 roots) (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6G–J.

claim: BFA-induced PIN2-GFP agglomerations persisted in emo1-RNAi after washout (washout efficiency: 39%).
source: While the PIN2-containing BFA compartments efficiently disappeared in wild-type root epidermal cells (washout efficiency: 66%, n ≥ 100 cells, 20 roots), BFA-induced PIN2-GFP agglomerations persisted in emo1-RNAi (washout efficiency: 39%, n ≥ 100 cells, 20 roots) (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6G–J.

claim: Reduced expression of the 14-3-3 epsilon members interferes with PIN2 recycling events to the PM.
source: Taken together, reduced expression of the 14-3-3 epsilon members interferes with PIN2 recycling events to the PM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on BFA washout experiments.

claim: The Rab5-like GTPase ARA7 marks a subdomain of the TGN but mostly accumulates at the MVBs.
source: The Rab5-like GTPase ARA7 marks a subdomain of the TGN but mostly accumulates at the MVBs (Singh et al., 2014) that become vacuolated in the presence of wortmannin (Robinson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Robinson et al., 2008.

claim: The size of ARA7-containing wortmannin-induced compartments displaying ring-shaped structures was remarkably reduced in emo1-RNAi as compared to the wild type.
source: While striking differences could not be observed in the absence of inhibitor, the size of ARA7-containing wortmannin-induced compartments displaying ring-shaped structures was remarkably reduced in emo1-RNAi as compared to the wild type (Figure 7A–G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A–G.

claim: Enlargement of ARA7-positive organelles is characteristic of mutants such as gnom, vps29 and sand, which are affected in diverse post-Golgi trafficking processes but all interfere with vacuolar targeting.
source: Enlargement of ARA7-positive organelles is, however, characteristic of mutants such as gnom (impaired recycling: [Geldner et al., 2003]), vps29 (impaired retrograde trafficking: [Jaillais et al., 2007]) and sand (impaired MVB-vacuole fusion: [Singh et al., 2014]), which are affected in diverse post-Golgi trafficking processes but all interfere (indirectly or directly) with vacuolar targeting.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geldner et al., 2003; Jaillais et al., 2007; and Singh et al., 2014.

claim: Endosomal trafficking to the tonoplast membrane is significantly delayed in emo1-RNAi in comparison to the wild type.
source: Accordingly, we revealed through pulse labeling by FM4-64 and sequential treatments of cycloheximide and BFA that endosomal trafficking to the tonoplast membrane is significantly delayed in emo1-RNAi in comparison to the wild type (Figure 7H–N).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 pulse-chase data shown in Figure 7H–N.

claim: The retarded trafficking of FM4-64 and thus, of PM material in general, to the vacuole is also evident in the absence of BFA.
source: The retarded trafficking of FM4-64 and thus, of PM material in general, to the vacuole is also evident in the absence of BFA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 trafficking data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: emo1-RNAi exhibits an increase in the total PIN2-GFP levels in membrane protein preparations in the presence of ethanol.
source: Consistent with the observed effects on vacuolar trafficking, emo1-RNAi exhibits an increase in the total PIN2-GFP levels in membrane protein preparations in the presence of ethanol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H), while transcript levels remain unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: PIN2-GFP transcript levels remain unaltered in emo1-RNAi.
source: Consistent with the observed effects on vacuolar trafficking, emo1-RNAi exhibits an increase in the total PIN2-GFP levels in membrane protein preparations in the presence of ethanol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H), while transcript levels remain unaltered.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: At the cellular level, the absence of 14-3-3 epsilon group members entailed disturbance of at least two endocytic trafficking pathways: from the TGN to the vacuole and to the PM.
source: At the cellular level, the absence of 14-3-3 epsilon group members did hence entail disturbance of at least two endocytic trafficking pathways: from the TGN to the vacuole and to the PM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple trafficking experiments.

claim: The level of PIN2-GFP is elevated in intracellular vesicular structures of emo1-RNAi.
source: We thus assumed the level of PIN2-GFP to be elevated in intracellular vesicular structures of emo1-RNAi.
evidence: This is an inference based on trafficking defects and protein accumulation data.

claim: In contrast to the wild type, considerable levels of PIN2-GFP are detectable in endosomal structures in emo1-RNAi following short-term treatment (10 min) with BFA concentrations as low as 10 μM.
source: Indeed, in contrast to the wild type, considerable levels of PIN2-GFP are detectable in endosomal structures in emo1-RNAi following short-term treatment (10 min) with BFA concentrations as low as 10 μM (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A,D.

claim: Auxins such as NAA inhibit endocytosis but do not interfere with the BFA-induced formation of endosomal BFA compartments.
source: Auxins such as NAA inhibit endocytosis but do not interfere with the BFA-induced formation of endosomal BFA compartments (Paciorek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paciorek et al., 2005.

claim: In contrast to the wild type, PIN2-GFP localized to BFA compartments of emo1-RNAi root epidermal cells when pretreated with FM4-64 and NAA.
source: When pretreated with FM4-64 (5 min), we observed a reduced frequency and size of FM-stained BFA bodies in NAA (and CHX)-treated plants. Nonetheless, in contrast to the wild type, PIN2-GFP localized to BFA compartments of emo1-RNAi root epidermal cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I–M), strongly supporting an increased PIN2-GFP content in endosomal structures.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I–M.

claim: The finding clearly points to an accumulation of PIN2-GFP in endosomal vesicles such as early/recycling endosomes and MVBs.
source: Taken together, our finding clearly points to an accumulation of PIN2-GFP in endosomal vesicles such as early/recycling endosomes and MVBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple trafficking experiments.

claim: The 14-3-3 epsilon group members localize to post Golgi compartments.
source: Since trafficking processes were affected by the RNAi approach, we wondered whether the respective 14-3-3 isoforms localize to post Golgi compartments. Indeed, they do since BFA clearly induced the accumulation of epsilon group members in BFA bodies (mu: Figure 1R,S).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1R,S.

claim: Several well-characterized 14-3-3 interactors were identified by MS, among those different isoforms of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase.
source: As expected, several well-characterized 14-3-3 interactors were identified by MS (highlighted in green in Table 1—source data 1), among those different isoforms of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data presented in Table 1—source data 1.

claim: A remarkable number of proteins known or assumed to be involved in membrane trafficking processes co-precipitated with epsilon-GFP but not GFP alone.
source: Furthermore, a remarkable number of proteins known or assumed to be involved in membrane trafficking processes co-precipitated with epsilon-GFP but not GFP alone (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data presented in Table 1.

claim: Small GTPases (subfamily RAB) and their effector proteins (subfamilies ARF and RAB), required for vesicle formation (ARF) and tethering (RAB) co-precipitated with epsilon-GFP.
source: These include small GTPases (subfamily RAB) and their effector proteins (subfamilies ARF and RAB), required for vesicle formation (ARF) and tethering (RAB) (Park and Jürgens, 2011; Vernoud et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and citations to Park and Jürgens, 2011 and Vernoud et al., 2003.

claim: AtTRS130 has been suggested to act upstream of RAB-A GTPases in post-Golgi membrane trafficking.
source: Likewise, AtTRS130 has been suggested to act upstream of RAB-A GTPases in post-Golgi membrane trafficking (Qi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qi et al., 2011.

claim: Adaptors of membrane vesicle coat proteins involved in clathrin-related endomembrane trafficking in plants (ENTH/ANTH/VHS superfamily proteins) co-precipitated with epsilon-GFP.
source: In addition, adaptors of membrane vesicle coat proteins involved in clathrin-related endomembrane trafficking in plants (ENTH/ANTH/VHS superfamily proteins) (Zouhar and Sauer, 2014), proteins essential for vesicle fusion, such as regulators of SNAREs (e.g. SEC1B) and a regulator of the MVB pathway (IST1-LIKE 3) were identified as putative epsilon interactors (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data presented in Table 1 and citation to Zouhar and Sauer, 2014.

claim: Proteins essential for vesicle fusion, such as regulators of SNAREs (e.g. SEC1B) and a regulator of the MVB pathway (IST1-LIKE 3) were identified as putative epsilon interactors.
source: In addition, adaptors of membrane vesicle coat proteins involved in clathrin-related endomembrane trafficking in plants (ENTH/ANTH/VHS superfamily proteins) (Zouhar and Sauer, 2014), proteins essential for vesicle fusion, such as regulators of SNAREs (e.g. SEC1B) and a regulator of the MVB pathway (IST1-LIKE 3) were identified as putative epsilon interactors (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data presented in Table 1.

claim: The list of potential epsilon interactors strongly suggests a direct regulation of cellular trafficking by 14-3-3 proteins.
source: The list of potential epsilon interactors thus strongly suggests a direct regulation of cellular trafficking by 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the identification of trafficking-related proteins as interactors.

claim: Conditional knockdown of the entire 14-3-3 epsilon group in Arabidopsis seedlings led to pronounced defects in PIN polar distribution and associated auxin-mediated plant development.
source: Here, we tackle this question by conditional knockdown of the entire 14-3-3 epsilon group in Arabidopsis seedlings (three of the five isoforms are expressed in seedlings). Interference with their function led to pronounced defects in PIN polar distribution and associated auxin-mediated plant development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the entire study.

claim: In vivo visualization of endocytic cargo revealed defects in defined post-Golgi trafficking processes.
source: At the cellular level, in vivo visualization of endocytic cargo revealed defects in defined post-Golgi trafficking processes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on FM4-64 and BFA experiments.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins co-immunoprecipitated with several factors crucial for membrane trafficking, suggesting that lack of these interactions might underlie the mutant phenotype.
source: 14-3-3 proteins co-immunoprecipitated with several factors crucial for membrane trafficking, suggesting that lack of these interactions might underlie the mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The epsilon group may have retained functional characteristics of the ancestral eukaryotic 14-3-3 protein.
source: The epsilon group may have retained functional characteristics of the ancestral eukaryotic 14-3-3 protein.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on phylogenetic analysis and functional data.

claim: Potential roles of yeast 14-3-3 in vesicular transport have been proposed.
source: Potential roles of yeast 14-3-3 in vesicular transport have been proposed (Gelperin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gelperin et al., 1995.

claim: Proteome-wide surveys of the mammalian 14-3-3 interactome unequivocally revealed links to regulation of cellular trafficking, organization and membrane dynamics.
source: Furthermore, proteome-wide surveys of the mammalian 14-3-3 interactome unequivocally revealed links to regulation of cellular trafficking, organization and membrane dynamics (Pozuelo Rubio et al., 2004; Jin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pozuelo Rubio et al., 2004 and Jin et al., 2004.

claim: 14-3-3 binding overcomes ER retention in yeast and mammals and thus positively affects forward transport of certain membrane proteins, in particular channels, in the secretory pathway.
source: The molecular interactions and proper mechanisms are, however, still poorly understood with one prominent exception: 14-3-3 binding overcomes ER retention in yeast and mammals and thus positively affects forward transport of certain membrane proteins, in particular channels, in the secretory pathway (review: [Mrowiec and Schwappach, 2006])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mrowiec and Schwappach, 2006.

claim: In plants, large-scale experiments searching for putative 14-3-3 interactors have mostly been performed by using non-epsilon isoforms that predominantly impact primary metabolism.
source: In plants, large-scale experiments searching for putative 14-3-3 interactors have mostly been performed by using non-epsilon isoforms that predominantly impact primary metabolism (Shin et al., 2011), ion homeostasis and signal mediators (Chang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shin et al., 2011 and Chang et al., 2009.

claim: Regulation of intracellular trafficking events by plant 14-3-3 proteins has not even been considered prior to this study.
source: Therefore, regulation of intracellular trafficking events by plant 14-3-3 proteins has not even been considered.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Interference with the function of Arabidopsis epsilon group members clearly evidenced a reduced polar localization of PIN proteins and defects in endocytic trafficking pathways.
source: Interference with the function of Arabidopsis epsilon group members now clearly evidenced a reduced polar localization of PIN proteins and defects in endocytic trafficking pathways.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the entire study.

claim: Endocytic trafficking (TGN to vacuole) of PM material, in general, is delayed in emo1-RNAi as shown by the experiments performed with the endocytic tracer FM4-64.
source: In fact, endocytic trafficking (TGN to vacuole) of PM material, in general, is delayed as shown by the experiments performed with the endocytic tracer FM4-64.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on FM4-64 trafficking experiments.

claim: The predominance of auxin transport-dependent phenotypes most likely is caused by the strong impact of auxin distribution on plant growth and development.
source: The predominance of auxin transport-dependent phenotypes most likely is caused by the strong impact of auxin distribution on plant growth and development.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: The molecular mechanisms regulating intracellular transport, such as vesicle formation, budding, delivery, tethering and fusion, are complex and not well understood in plants.
source: The molecular mechanisms regulating intracellular transport, such as vesicle formation, budding, delivery, tethering and fusion, are complex and not well understood in plants.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Large protein families, among those small GTPases and their regulators, are crucial factors of vesicle trafficking pathways.
source: Large protein families, among those small GTPases and their regulators, are crucial factors of vesicle trafficking pathways (Park and Jürgens, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park and Jürgens, 2011.

claim: Lack of interactions between 14-3-3 and trafficking-related proteins might be responsible for the phenotypes observed in emo-RNAi lines.
source: It is, nonetheless, obvious that lack of these interactions might be responsible for the phenotypes observed in emo-RNAi lines.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Small GTPases and their regulators represent ideal targets of 14-3-3 epsilon members due to their evolutionarily conserved function throughout eukaryotes.
source: Small GTPases and their regulators, for instance, represent ideal targets of 14-3-3 epsilon members due to their evolutionarily conserved function throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on evolutionary conservation.

claim: The clustering analysis of in vivo 14-3-3-binding proteins in mammals argues for significant control of small GTPase pathways by phospho-dependent 14-3-3 interactions.
source: Remarkably, the clustering analysis of in vivo 14-3-3-binding proteins in mammals argues for significant control of small GTPase pathways by phospho-dependent 14-3-3 interactions (Jin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2004.

claim: The results provide clear evidence for the involvement of 14-3-3 epsilon members in regulating the subcellular polarity of PIN proteins, endocytic membrane trafficking processes and auxin-dependent growth in Arabidopsis.
source: In conclusion, our results provide clear evidence for the involvement of 14-3-3 epsilon members in regulating the subcellular polarity of PIN proteins, endocytic membrane trafficking processes and auxin-dependent growth in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.
